cur:catacombs-arles-marcia-romania-celsa.summary: Under a lid with a central inscription and scenes of the Nativity and the Magi, the front unrolls a long frieze of miracles, with Christ repeatedly touching and healing among the crowd. It was made for a woman named Marcia Romania Celsa.
facts: The museum states that it was discovered in 1974, like the 'Trinity' sarcophagus.
Its lid combines an inscription panel with small figured scenes, a common arrangement on Roman frieze sarcophagi.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-119-chris.summary: With his back turned, the psalmist stands on a hillock and calls on the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who appears half-length in the heavens: 'in my distress I cried unto the Lord, and he heard me'. Around him are men with flaming arrows — 'sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper' — the dwellers of Kedar, and in a cave the people of lying lips and deceitful tongue. It is the first of the fifteen Songs of Ascents.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-119-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects-bargello-ascension-triptych-.summary: At the top, Christ sits in a round glory borne aloft by two angels with outspread wings; below, between two stylised trees and beneath a Greek inscription, and the twelve apostles with the Virgin stand gazing upward. The clear division between heaven above and earth below expresses the meaning of the feast: the Lord who ascends will return in glory.
facts: The panel was the centre of a triptych, whose hinged wings would have closed over it (type).

The Ascension, celebrated forty days after Easter, was one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine Church and is often shown, as here, with the Virgin standing among the apostles (iconographic tradition).

cur:objects-pushkin-constantine-vii-crow.summary: Christ, standing on a footstool and identified by the letters IC XC, lays his hand upon the crown of the emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, who bows slightly before him in jewelled imperial dress. Inscriptions name the emperor as autokrator. The plaque makes visible the Byzantine conviction that the emperor's authority came directly from Christ.
facts: The plaque is usually dated around 945, when Constantine VII became sole emperor after the deposition of the Lekapenos family.
It belongs to a small group of imperial ivories, together with the Romanos Ivory in Paris, showing Christ crowning the ruler (comparison).

Q116273568.summary: This small Byzantine ivory casket carries on its lid a Deësis: Christ enthroned in majesty between the Virgin and John the Forerunner, with archangels, all set in roundels linked by delicate scrollwork. Around the sides the twelve apostles appear in medallion portraits, each named in carefully carved Greek letters. Made to hold relics, it surrounds its sacred contents with the heavenly court interceding before Christ.
facts: Greek inscriptions name every figure: Paul, Peter, James and Andrew on the front, Philip and Thomas, John, Mark, Luke and Matthew, Bartholomew and Simon on the other sides, and John the Baptist, Jesus Christ and the Mother of God on the lid.
Its recorded history begins with Pope Innocent IV (Sinibaldo Fieschi); it later passed through the Heckscher and Oppenheim collections to J. Pierpont Morgan.
It was shown in the Met's landmark exhibition 'The Glory of Byzantium' (1997).
Q116273568.notes: Met 17.190.238, 950–1000, probably Constantinople. The Met lists Mark and Luke among the apostles on the back; no scripture is given because the Deësis is not a narrative scene.
